scenario: AITA for refusing an additional guest at our wedding | Thanks for watching this post. First time writing here and non-native English speaker. I am getting married very soon. As you can imagine, this takes a lot of preparation. I'm talking here about the civil wedding, which will be very intimate and consequently restricted to our very close family: parents, siblings and, in my case, godparents and their children. The wedding will happen in another country, so this takes a lot of preparation as it is in another culture. When I made the invitations, I've been clear: I invited my parents (2 p.) and my godparents' family (4 p.). I've been very flexible, I told everyone that they could join us anytime they like (i.e., arrive in the country when they wish because I understand it's complicated when you have 4 different jobs etc) as long as they'll be present for the ceremony. Moreover, because the destination is far, my in-laws kindly proposed to offer the accommodation to all of them. The wedding is now in one month and I just received a message from my godmother saying that they have booked the flights, and they will be 5 because the gf of my cousin is joining. That's where I am really feeling uncomfortable: I receive this as a 'fait accompli' (done deal) without any prior consultation, without even asking me if that's ok to have an additional person (that I've never met). I've always been clear about the number of people invited. I just can't stand to receive this kind of 'news' via a late evening text message. It's not that I'm against that additional person. It's just the way that I'm put in front of this, as if I had nothing to say. And we're not talking about the 'party' wedding, but something very special that is meant to be in strict intimacy. Moreover, I know that they have their tickets since 1 month, and I was waiting for their news to plan the trip etc. So they literally waited 1 month to announce it, now that the date is getting closer. I just don't understand this kind of behavior. It costs nothing to make a quick phone call before booking anything, and to ask if it's possible, etc. In sum, they just invited someone at my wedding, someone that wasn't ever planned and that I don't even know. This morning, I sent a polite message saying: 'I'm confused by your news, I've always been clear about the number of guests and why I picked these specific guests (i.e. you) for our wedding. Why haven't you called me and asked me before booking anything? I'm put in front of a done deal, and I have to oppose myself to it, as it goes against the very idea of what we've been planning for months. The solution to this situation, I am afraid, does not lie within my hands. If X is feeling uncomfortable about this, I could understand, but with respect to my in-laws, I just cannot accept this compromise.' So: Am I the asshole? More precisely: Am I the asshole for refusing this, for writing to them clearly that it will not be possible and that they should have contacted me before doing anything? Thanks.

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.
Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

Let’s break this down objectively to address whether your response was appropriate or not, considering cultural, social, and interpersonal dynamics. --- ### **Key Points to Consider:** 1. **Clarity in Invitations:** You were **explicit** about the guest list (intimate, specific people) and the conditions (e.g., arrival flexibility, ceremony attendance). This sets clear expectations, and your godmother’s action violates that clarity. **This is not unreasonable.** 2. **Lack of Communication:** The fact that they booked flights for an additional guest **without consulting you** is disrespectful. A simple call or message to ask, *"Can we bring [person]?"* would have been a basic courtesy. Their behavior suggests **entitlement**—assuming your invitation was open-ended despite your clear boundaries. 3. **Cultural Context:** - In some cultures, weddings are highly communal, and family dynamics may prioritize group harmony over individual boundaries. However, **your wedding is explicitly intimate**, which is a valid choice. You’re not obligated to accommodate last-minute additions just because it’s a "family" event. - The fact that they’re in another country adds complexity, but **that doesn’t excuse bypassing your rules**. If they had questions, they should have asked you directly. 4. **Your Response:** Your message strikes the right balance: - **Polite but firm**: You acknowledge their kindness (in-laws offering accommodation) while standing your ground. - **Clear about boundaries**: You explain why the guest list is fixed and why their approach was problematic. - **No compromise**: You refuse to bend, which is fair given the situation. You’re not being unreasonable—you’re upholding your own plans. 5. **Is This "Asshole Behavior"?** - **No, you are not the asshole.** You’re the one who set clear rules and communicated them. Their behavior (booking flights without asking) is the asshole move here. - **However**, if this is part of a larger pattern (e.g., repeated disrespect), it might reflect deeper issues in how they handle boundaries. But in this isolated incident, **your reaction is justified**. 6. **Alternative Perspectives (Why They Might Have Done This):** - **Overconfidence**: They assumed you’d be too polite to refuse (a common mistake in cultures where direct "no" is rare). - **Lack of awareness**: They may not realize how much effort you’ve put into planning an intimate wedding. - **Family pressure**: Sometimes, extended family pushes for more guests, but that doesn’t give them the right to unilaterally change your plans. 7. **What Could Have Been Done Differently?** - **Early in the planning**, you could have explicitly stated: *"If anyone has questions about the guest list, please ask me directly—this is a very personal celebration."* - **If they had asked**, you could have explained your reasoning (e.g., *"This is a small, meaningful gathering for our closest family"*). --- ### **Final Verdict: 1 (Not the Asshole)** You are **not** the asshole. Your response was: - **Respectful** (you didn’t insult them). - **Consistent** (you stuck to your original plan). - **Proactive** (you communicated your discomfort clearly). Their behavior was **disrespectful of your boundaries**, and refusing their addition is entirely reasonable. If they had asked first, you might have been more flexible, but **they didn’t ask**—they presented a fait accompli. --- ### **What to Do Next?** 1. **Stand firm**: If they push back, reiterate that the guest list is final. You can say: *"I understand this is disappointing, but the wedding is planned around these numbers. If you’d like to discuss alternatives (e.g., a separate gathering), I’m open to it."* 2. **Document the conversation**: Keep a record of your messages in case there’s confusion later. 3. **Prepare for reactions**: Some family members might feel hurt or offended. Be ready to explain that this is about honoring your vision for the day. 4. **Focus on the positive**: This is a small hiccup in a big celebration. Your wedding is about **you and your closest people**—that’s a beautiful choice. --- ### **Cultural Note:** In some cultures, weddings are seen as a time for **family unity**, and individual boundaries might be secondary. However, **your wedding is your day**, and you have every right to set the rules. If this is a recurring issue, it might be worth having a **calmer, separate conversation** with your godparents about how to handle future plans together. But for now, **you’re in the right**. Would you like help drafting a follow-up message if they push back?
